issues.legal_issue: Legislation that changes a voluntary association’s membership without the existing members’ consent interferes with the right to form and continue the association.
material_facts: The society was voluntarily formed, and its rules placed the choice of new members with its own working committee.
The legislation made existing society members members of a statutory body but also added other persons without giving existing members a choice to accept or reject them.
The legislation empowered a government-constituted governing body to make broad rules for future membership, and the rules allowed further members to join without the original members’ consent.
The statutory body’s formation was the basis for the legislation’s other provisions.
issues.conclusion: The legislation’s compulsory reconstitution of the society violated the original members’ right to form an association. The restriction was not justified under the permitted grounds, and because the new body’s formation was the basis of the legislation, the Act was invalid as a whole.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(c) protects not only the initial formation of an association but also its continuation with the membership voluntarily agreed upon by its members. A law that imposes members on an association without giving existing members an option to exclude them, or removes members who voluntarily joined, infringes that right. Article 19(4) permits restrictions only in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, public order, or morality; no such justification applied. The Court relied on O.K. Ghosh v. E.X. Joseph, State of Madras v. V.G. Row, and V.G. Row v. The State of Madras.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_associationa: A constitutional challenge concerns legislation that restructures a voluntary association.
predicates.voluntary_association_has_member_selecti: The association’s members formed it voluntarily under rules governing who could join.
predicates.legislation_imposes_members_without_exis: The legislation adds members without allowing existing members to accept or reject them.
predicates.legislation_changes_association_composit: The legislation changes who belongs to the association rather than merely regulating its administration.
predicates.no_permissible_associational_justificati: The change is not shown to serve a constitutionally permitted ground for restricting the association right.
predicates.compulsory_reconstitution_violates_assoc: The compulsory change to the association’s membership violates the right to form and continue the association.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns legislation that changes the composition of a voluntarily formed association by imposing members without the existing members’ choice, and no permitted justification applies, the compulsory reconstitution violates the associational right.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament lacks legislative competence to legislate for a newly created body when the national-importance declaration covered only a distinct pre-existing institution.
material_facts: The legislation declared the existing society to be an institution of national importance and relied on that declaration as the basis for Parliament’s legislative authority.
On the alternative interpretation that the society continued to exist, the legislation created a separate corporate body and transferred the society’s functions and property to it.
The newly created body itself had not been declared an institution of national importance.
issues.conclusion: On the alternative interpretation that the society remained intact and a separate body was created, Parliament was not competent to legislate for that new body on the basis of the declaration concerning the society.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 63 of List I of the Seventh Schedule empowered Parliament to legislate concerning institutions declared by law to be of national importance. The declaration covered the society, not a separate newly created body. The Court also noted that the constitution of societies fell within List II. The required declaration could not be extended from the society to a distinct body merely because the two had the same name.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_legislative_: A constitutional challenge disputes the legislature’s authority to legislate for a body.
predicates.legislation_claims_authority_from_nation: The legislation relies on a declaration that an institution is of national importance as the basis for legislative authority.
predicates.new_body_is_distinct_from_declared_insti: The body addressed by the legislation is a separate legal entity from the institution covered by the declaration.
predicates.only_predecessor_is_declared_nationally_: The declaration applies to the pre-existing institution and not to the separate new body.
predicates.parliament_lacks_legislative_competence_: Parliament lacks legislative competence over the distinct body on the basis of the declaration concerning the pre-existing institution.

issues.definition: If a legislative-competence challenge concerns a distinct new body and the relied-on national-importance declaration covers only its predecessor, Parliament lacks competence over the new body on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: Transferring all of an existing society’s property to a distinct body while leaving the society in existence is not a reasonable restriction on the right to hold property.
material_facts: On the alternative interpretation considered by the Court, the original society remained in existence while a new, separate corporate body received its property and assets.
The property had vested in the society’s governing body under the Societies Registration Act, 1860.
The transfer deprived the society and the persons in whom its property vested of the property altogether, rather than regulating its management or preservation.
The society’s affairs were in difficulty, but the legislation’s transfer was not limited to ensuring proper management or preservation.
issues.conclusion: On the assumption that the society continued to exist, the total transfer of its property to a distinct body violated the right to hold property and could not be justified as a reasonable restriction in the public interest.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) protected the right to hold property, subject to reasonable restrictions in the public interest under Article 19(5). A law directed to proper management or preservation may impose restrictions, but total deprivation of property is not justified merely as a management measure. Under section 5 of the Societies Registration Act, 1860, the property vested in the society’s governing body. The Court distinguished The Board of Trustees, Ayurvedic and Unani Tibia College, Delhi v. The State of Delhi because that case proceeded on the basis that the original society’s property did not vest in its members after the board was dissolved.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_tra: A constitutional challenge concerns legislation transferring property held for an existing society.
predicates.existing_society_continues_to_exist: The society remains in existence after the transfer.
predicates.property_vested_in_existing_holders: The property is vested in the society or persons who hold it for the society.
predicates.all_property_transferred_to_distinct_bod: The legislation transfers the society’s property altogether to a separate body.

issues.definition: When an existing society’s property is vested in its holders but is transferred altogether to a distinct body, leaving those holders totally deprived and without a management or preservation measure, the transfer violates the right to hold property.
